author: Carlos Pérez
title: “Esto no para”: Una perspectiva de base sobre la huelga indefinida por la educación pública en Madrid
content:
“Esto no para”: Una perspectiva de base sobre la huelga indefinida por la educación pública en Madrid




Desde el 14 de octubre, las docentes de Madrid, España, se encuentran en huelga indefinida en defensa de la educación pública. Tras años de deterioro de las condiciones laborales y una organización sistemática de las bases, las docentes han inundado las calles de la capital española en una movilización masiva que ha vinculado la lucha por la educación pública con la reciente revuelta en torno a la vivienda.




La lucha conjunta por la vivienda y la educación pública en España se encamina ahora hacia una huelga general el 11 de noviembre, en medio de un levantamiento más amplio que se extiende por toda Europa.




Carlos Pérez, maestro de estudios sociales en Carolina del Norte y miembro de la junta directiva de Labor Notes habló con María, profesora de secundaria de historia y geografía en Madrid y militante de Menos Lectivas, una de las principales fuerzas de base detrás de la huelga.




Pérez: Los docentes de la escuela pública en Madrid mantienen una huelga indefinida desde el 14 de octubre. ¿Cuáles son los motivos principales que les llevaron a usted y a otros docentes a convocar una huelga, y cuáles son sus reivindicaciones?




María:

 En la Comunidad de Madrid venimos arrastrando recortes en la educación pública desde el año 2011. Estos han ido deteriorando el estado de las aulas y la calidad educativa de los estudiantes madrileños. 




La falta de recursos y de personal, la cantidad de alumnos en el aula, el aumento de horas lectivas (horas de clase directa en el aula) y la falta de mantenimiento y construcción de infraestructuras nos han dejado un escenario en el que impartir clase es muy complicado. Las docentes no llegamos a atender a todos nuestros estudiantes y hemos decidido plantarnos ante el maltrato institucional que sufrimos tanto nosotras como nuestro alumnado.




En mi caso, he dado clase a aulas de bachillerato con 33 alumnos, he tenido que buscar un aula donde meter a mis alumnos cada día durante un mes de lluvias intensas porque las aulas tenían unas goteras que provocan que estuviesen constantemente mojadas; mis alumnos con necesidades educativas (autismo o dificultades de audición y lenguaje) no han sido atendidos por las profesionales que hacían falta porque no había ni integradora social ni profesora específica para ellos, y por supuesto trabajo una cantidad de horas extra ingentes y no están remuneradas ni reconocidas. 




Por eso reivindicamos y exigimos a la Comunidad de Madrid que reduzca las horas lectivas; reducir los ratios entre las docentes y alumnos; acabar con la segregación, dado que la Comunidad de Madrid es la región de España más segregada en educación; aumentar el salario para equiparlo a las necesidades económicas actuales; reducir la burocracia, entre otras cosas. 




Menos Lectivas, una plataforma de base que agrupa a varios sindicatos, ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la huelga. ¿Qué es Menos Lectivas y qué papel ha desempeñado en este conflicto?




Menos Lectivas nace en el 2023, inspirada por colectivos como Labor Notes en los EEUU, con la intención de organizar a las trabajadoras de la educación desde los centros de trabajo y devolver el poder sindical a las trabajadoras. Desde entonces hemos construido nuestro movimiento a través de asambleas de centro. 




En estos años previos a la huelga indefinida se han convocado huelgas, manifestaciones y concentraciones que han servido para que cada vez el movimiento fuese más grande y, sobre todo, tuviésemos legitimidad institucional — tanto con los trabajadores que nos ven como un agente de lucha válido porque se sienten parte de él gracias a las asambleas, como para el resto de sindicatos, los medios de comunicación y en última instancia los gobiernos — para decidir cómo, cuándo y dónde queríamos luchar por el derecho a la educación y nuestros derechos laborales.




Desde los inicios sabíamos que la huelga indefinida sería la última herramienta de lucha sindical si nuestras demandas no eran escuchadas por la Comunidad de Madrid y, el pasado junio, se decidió en asamblea que las docentes iríamos a la huelga indefinida. Siendo ya un conjunto de asambleas con legitimidad el resto de sindicatos que no formaban parte de Menos Lectivas tuvieron que sentarse con nosotras en el Comité de Huelga a negociar la constitución de una mesa de negociación y las condiciones de la huelga. Este hito ya es un éxito, consiguiendo que el poder vuelva a las trabajadoras y salga de los despachos.




¿Cómo ha sido recibida la huelga por parte del alumnado y sus familias?




Tanto las familias como el alumnado están de acuerdo con nuestras reivindicaciones. En última instancia, son los principales beneficiarios de las mejoras que consigamos. Nos sentimos muy apoyadas por ellos y son una parte esencial de la lucha.




Los estudiantes organizados han convocado también huelga indefinida a través de distintos partidos y organizaciones políticas como el Sindicato de Estudiantes o la Organización Estudiantil Socialista. Están presentes en todas las acciones que hacemos en las calles y forman una parte importante de la lucha por la educación. 




Las familias, por su parte, se organizan en asociaciones de familias en cada uno de los centros educativos y en los barrios y ayudan a sostener las cajas de resistencia. Además, han convocado una concentración propia para hacerle ver a la Consejera de Educación que esta lucha no es exclusiva de las docentes, si no también de las familias.




Dado que la huelga es indefinida, ¿qué tipo de tácticas han empleado para mantener la participación colectiva y la presión? 




Estamos en la calle constantemente, concentraciones, manifestaciones, performances, asambleas y ocupando el espacio suficiente como para que los medios se hagan eco de nuestras reivindicaciones. 




Es importante que toda la ciudadanía nos vea y nos escuche para que sean conscientes de la realidad de las aulas. En cuanto son conscientes de ella, se unen a la lucha, como mencioné con los estudiantes y sus familias.




Esta huelga tiene lugar bajo el gobierno progresista de Pedro Sánchez, del Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE). ¿Cómo ha respondido el gobierno de Sánchez ante la huelga?




El pasado 5 de octubre el presidente del Gobierno convocó elecciones generales en España, por lo que está huelga ha entrado dentro de su campaña electoral. No les ha quedado otra que mostrar su apoyo a las docentes madrileñas. 




Sin embargo, en los 8 años que el PSOE lleva gobernando en España, no han hecho nada por mejorar las condiciones del profesorado ni del alumnado. Desde el gobierno se limpian las manos y argumentan que las competencias en Educación son de las Comunidades Autónomas pero el Ministerio de Educación y el Gobierno Central son responsables tanto de las condiciones de los trabajadores como de la educación de todos los españoles. 




Además, la Delegación de Gobierno, que pertenece y dirige al Gobierno central y que controla la Policía Nacional, no está dando explicaciones sobre las brutales cargas policiales que hemos sufrido, tanto los docentes como los alumnos, durante las manifestaciones y concentraciones de este último mes.




La huelga en la enseñanza pública coincide con un movimiento masivo en torno a la vivienda, tanto en Madrid como en otros lugares. ¿Hasta qué punto están vinculadas ambas luchas?




Menos Lectivas siempre ha estado muy unida con el Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid. Hace un año se empezó a desarrollar el protocolo “Sin vivienda no hay educación” en distintos institutos de la Comunidad de Madrid con el fin de que las familias y alumnado que tuviesen una situación de vivienda precaria o se fuesen a enfrentar a un desahucio supiesen cómo actuar y pudiésemos atajarlo no solo desde el sindicato sino también desde los centros educativos. 




Lo que refleja esta situación es que la socialdemocracia supeditada al neoliberalismo no está garantizando que los trabajadores tengan sus necesidades básicas cubiertas y este hecho está provocando una oleada de protestas y huelgas en toda Europa. España no es una excepción.. El maltrato de los servicios públicos, como educación o sanidad, y la mala gestión del problema de la vivienda en España están siendo el talón de Aquiles del “gobierno más progresista de la historia”.




¿Qué logros han obtenido ya gracias a la huelga y qué lecciones están surgiendo a medida que esta avanza?




En el momento en el que se hace esta entrevista, la consejera de educación de la Comunidad de Madrid se sigue negando a negociar con el comité de huelga. Llevamos ya más de dos semanas de huelga. 




Pero sabemos que hemos conseguido dotar de fuerza a las trabajadoras para luchar por una mejora en sus condiciones laborales. Hemos conseguido devolver el foco a las aulas y mostrar cuál es la realidad de la educación pública, mostrando que el gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid no tiene ninguna intención de sostenerla. Hemos conseguido organizarnos y vamos a conseguir ganar. Esto no para.

author: Carlos Pérez
title: ‘This Isn’t Stopping’: A Rank-And-File Perspective on the Indefinite Strike for Public Education in Madrid
content:
Since October 14, teachers in Madrid, Spain, have been on an indefinite strike in defense of public education. After years of deteriorating conditions and systematic rank-and-file organizing, teachers have flooded the streets of Spain’s capital in a mass mobilization that has linked the fight for public education with the recent revolt around housing. 




The shared struggle for housing and public education in Spain is now heading toward a general strike on November 11 in the midst of a broader uprising spreading throughout Europe. 




Carlos Pérez, a North Carolina high school social studies teacher and Labor Notes board member, spoke with María, a secondary school teacher of history and geography in Madrid and a member of 

Menos Lectivas

 (a group whose name means “Fewer Teaching Hours”), one of the leading rank-and-file forces behind the strike. 




Pérez: Public school teachers in Madrid have been on an indefinite strike since October 14. What are the main issues that drove you and other teachers to call for a strike and what are your demands?




María:

 In the Community of Madrid, we have been dealing with cuts to public education since 2011. These have led to the deterioration of classroom conditions and the quality of education for students in the region.




A lack of resources and staff, high student-to-teacher ratios, an increase in direct teaching hours, and a failure to maintain or build necessary infrastructure have created a situation where teaching has become extremely difficult. We, as educators, are unable to adequately attend to all our students, and we have decided to take a stand against the institutional mistreatment that both we and our students are subjected to. 




In my case, I’ve taught high school classes with 33 students; I had to find a classroom to accommodate my students every day for a month of heavy rain because the classrooms had leaks that kept them constantly wet; my students with special educational needs (autism or hearing and speech difficulties) were not supported by the necessary professionals because there was neither a social integration specialist nor a teacher specifically assigned to them; and of course, I work an enormous amount of unpaid and unrecognized overtime.




This is why we are demanding that the Community of Madrid reduce the number of instructional hours; lower the teacher-to-student ratios; end segregation, given that the Community of Madrid is the most segregated region in Spain in terms of education; increase salaries to bring them in line with current economic needs; and reduce bureaucracy, among other things.




Menos Lectivas

, a rank-and-file formation that includes several unions, has been a driving force behind the strike. What is Menos Lectivas and what role has it played in the strike?




Menos Lectivas

 was founded in 2023, inspired by groups like Labor Notes in the United States, with the goal of organizing education workers from within their workplaces and returning union power to the workers themselves. Since then, we have built our movement through assemblies held at individual workplaces.




In the years leading up to the indefinite strike, we organized strikes, demonstrations, and rallies. These actions helped the movement grow and, crucially, provided us with the institutional legitimacy—both with the workers, who view us as a legitimate force for struggle because they feel part of it through our assemblies, and with other unions, the media, and ultimately the government—to decide how, when, and where we would fight for the right to education and for our own labor rights.




From the outset, we knew that an indefinite strike would be our ultimate tool for union struggle if our demands went unheeded by the Community of Madrid. Last June, it was decided in an assembly that we, the teachers, would launch an indefinite strike.




Given that these assemblies held clear legitimacy, the other unions that were not part of 

Menos Lectivas

 had no choice but to sit down with us on the Strike Committee to negotiate the establishment of a formal negotiating table and the terms of the strike.. This milestone is already a success; it has shifted power back into the hands of the workers, taking it out of the administrative offices.




How has the strike been received by students and their families?




Both families and students support our demands. Ultimately, they are the primary beneficiaries of the improvements we achieve. We feel very well supported by them, and they are an essential part of the struggle.




Organized students have also called for an indefinite strike, acting through various political parties and organizations such as the 

Sindicato de Estudiantes

 (Students’ Union) and the 

Organización Estudiantil Socialista

 (Socialist Student Organization). They are present at all our street actions and play a significant role in the struggle for education.




Families, meanwhile, are organizing themselves into associations, both within individual educational institutions and across neighborhoods, and are helping to support strike funds. They have also organized a demonstration of their own to show the Minister of Education that this struggle is not limited to teachers, but also involves families.




Given that the strike is indefinite, what kind of tactics have you all used to maintain collective participation and pressure?




We are constantly out in the streets—holding rallies, demonstrations, performances, and assemblies—occupying enough space to ensure that the media takes note of our demands.




It is important for the public to see and hear us, so that they become aware of the reality inside our classrooms. Once they are aware of it, they join the struggle, as I mentioned with students and their families..




This strike is taking place under the progressive government of Pedro Sanchez from the Spanish Socialist Workers Party (

Partido Socialista Obrero Español

, PSOE). How has Sánchez’s government responded to the strike?




On October 5, the Prime Minister called for general elections in Spain, meaning this strike has now become part of an electoral campaign. They had no choice but to express their support for the teachers in Madrid.




However, throughout the eight years that the PSOE has been in power in Spain, they have done nothing to improve conditions for either teaching staff or students. The government washes its hands of the matter, arguing that jurisdiction over education lies with the Autonomous Communities; yet, the Ministry of Education and the central government remain responsible for both the working conditions of staff and the education of all Spaniards.




Also, the Government Delegation—which is part of and directed by the central government, and which oversees the National Police—has offered no explanation for the brutal police crackdowns that both teachers and students have endured during the demonstrations and rallies held over the past month.




The strike in public education is taking place during a mass uprising around housing in and beyond Madrid. To what extent have these two struggles been linked?




Menos Lectivas

 has always maintained a close relationship with the Madrid Tenants’ Union (

Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid

). A year ago, a shared plan titled “No Housing, No Education” was launched in various secondary schools across the Community of Madrid. Its purpose was to ensure that families and students facing precarious housing situations or the threat of eviction would know how to respond, allowing us to address these issues not only through the union but also in our schools.




This situation reveals that social democracy, subordinated to neoliberalism, is failing to ensure that workers’ basic needs are met, which is fueling a wave of protests and strikes across Europe. Spain is no exception.. The neglect of public services, such as education and health care, combined with the mismanagement of the housing crisis in Spain, has become the Achilles' heel of what has been described as the “most progressive government in history.”




What gains have you already seen from the strike and what lessons are already emerging as the strike advances?




At the time of this interview, the Madrid regional government’s Minister of Education continues to refuse to negotiate with the strike committee. We are now more than two weeks into the strike.




Yet, we know that we have succeeded in giving strength to the workers in their fight for better working conditions. We have managed to shift the focus back to the classrooms and reveal the reality of public education, demonstrating that the Madrid regional government has no intention of supporting education. We have succeeded in organizing ourselves and we are going to win. This isn’t stopping.

author: Ellen David Friedman
title: Steward’s Corner: Rethink the Scripted ‘Ask’
content:
You’re having a conversation with a co-worker, but inside you’re feeling icy dread. You’re talking through a script that ends with asking them to do a specific thing: sign a union card, wear a button, come to a meeting, vote for a strike. And sure enough, when you ask, a wall comes down.




The co-worker looks away, makes an excuse, and pins you as someone who is after something. You’re disappointed, confused about why it didn’t work, and afraid you’re not going to meet your goal.




Many of us feel nervous or awkward about asking a co-worker to do something. Sometimes we just need to push ourselves to do it. But if you’re being pressured to follow the script and get to a particular “ask” without finding out who this person is and moving at their pace, that’s a problem.




A co-worker you don’t yet have much of a relationship with may be turned off that you’re pressuring them to take an action that has already been decided on by others.




What can you do instead? Replace the “ask” (to take some predetermined action) with an invitation: “Hey, some of us are getting together to talk about this. You want to join us?” “Can we figure out how you can be part of the solution to this problem that you’re posing?”

author: Luis Fernando Mora Reyes
title: Cómo construimos nuestro programa de educación sindical
content:
A principios de este año, surgió un debate entre miembros de nuestro sindicato, la Unión Nacional de Trabajadores por Aplicación (UNTA), a raíz de un comunicado en redes sociales que condenaba el secuestro por parte de los Estados Unidos, del presidente venezolano Nicolás Maduro y que exigía: “la defensa de la soberanía, la autodeterminación de los pueblos y la paz en América Latina”. 




Entre las bases del sindicato hubo posicionamientos encontrados sobre el comunicado, lo que generó que en la consiguiente Asamblea Coordinadora (en este espacio se informa, se discute y se llega a acuerdos entre las representaciones nacionales y locales del sindicato) se discutiera abiertamente sobre el tema. Hubo fuertes discusiones en las que existieron puntos de vista opuestos. Sin embargo, siempre se extendieron las opiniones con respeto y camaradería. 




Desde el sindicato entendimos que era necesario contar con espacios de discusión y análisis que permitieran mejorar nuestras capacidades políticas y sindicales.  Como resultado, los miembros decidieron constituir el Consejo Político Nacional (CPN), un espacio dentro del sindicato para el debate y las capacitaciones sobre temas políticos, económicos, laborales, de género y de cuestiones sociales. 




De esta forma, la Secretaría de Formación y Cultura propuso, en el marco del CPN, una serie de talleres de formación y capacitación política y sindical para todas las personas afiliadas. Los talleres buscaron resolver tres puntos: 







pensar de forma colectiva sobre temas de importancia nacional e internacional; 




fortalecer nuestras habilidades como afiliados del sindicato; 




fomentar una mayor participación en el día a día. 







El programa está conformado por cuatro grandes ejes en función de las necesidades del sindicato y se extendió la invitación tanto a las personas afiliadas como a especialistas a participar como ponentes en alguno de los temas. 




TEMAS DE PRIORIDAD




Los cuatro ejes son: 







talleres sobre el Convenio 193 de la OIT;




talleres sobre comprensión e interpretación de los Estatutos sindicales de la organización;




talleres sobre elementos técnicos para administrar los espacios sindicales; 




talleres de afiliación/organización.







Debido a que la UNTA formó parte de las discusiones sobre el Convenio 193 en materia de trabajo decente en la economía de plataformas en junio de este año, surgió la necesidad de que todas las personas afiliadas conocieran y comprendieran la relevancia de este. La necesidad de esto radica en que, desde el sindicato, se ha impulsado la ratificación del Convenio 193 en México y en el mundo, ya que, a partir de esto, podrán hacerse mejoras a la ley vigente en materia de trabajo por aplicación de México. 




Respecto a los tres ejes restantes del programa de capacitaciones, estos se encuentran íntimamente ligados entre sí. Una persona afiliada que conoce sus Estatutos puede participar activamente en cualquier área del sindicato. Asimismo, es necesario que los actuales representantes del sindicato profundicen en el conocimiento de los Estatutos. De igual manera, para prevenir malentendidos entre las personas afiliadas y los representantes, así como para profesionalizar los procesos internos de la organización, resulta fundamental que todas las personas afiliadas a la UNTA conozcan diversos elementos técnicos para administrar los espacios sindicales. Finalmente, para continuar construyendo poder colectivo, es crucial que los mismos afiliados se consideren organizadores—y podemos fomentar eso mediante talleres de afiliación y organización sindical. 




CONVERSACIONES VIRTUALES




Debido a cuán grande es el territorio mexicano, así como a la naturaleza del trabajo por aplicación, las capacitaciones se han llevado a cabo de manera virtual. Es decir, algunas personas se conectan desde el celular cuando están haciendo un servicio o toman tiempo de trabajo para continuar formándose y capacitándose. Esta es una clara muestra de la convicción que existe entre las personas afiliadas para continuar capacitándose y desarrollando sus habilidades. No obstante, para no intervenir ni interrumpir la jornada de trabajo con tanta frecuencia, los talleres se llevan a cabo cada tres semanas los días jueves. Hasta este momento, terminamos con el primer tema (el Convenio 193) e iniciamos con el segundo (comprensión de los Estatutos). Lo más importante es que todas las personas afiliadas a la UNTA contemos con espacios para la discusión y el análisis político, en donde la pluralidad de ideas sea el eje central y no un impedimento para continuar con la conversación. El que las personas afiliadas al sindicato tomen la decisión de conectarse para continuar formándose es una muestra del liderazgo y la convicción de las bases. 




Cabe destacar que, al interior de las capacitaciones, para guiar las discusiones, se dejan cuatro preguntas guía por tema. Al final, cada representación local debe entregar a la Secretaría de Formación y Cultura un escrito breve en el que se responden de manera puntual las preguntas. Con estos ejercicios se ha buscado incentivar la participación y discusión de las bases, fortalecer la habilidad de exposición de los ponentes, y fomentar en los afiliados un sentido de pertenencia y respeto a su sindicato. Por ejemplo, en cuanto al tema de la comprensión de los Estatutos, con las discusiones, las preguntas guía y los documentos escritos por las bases pueden comenzar a plantearse cambios, mejoras o adecuaciones a los mismos. Esto también se hizo durante los talleres del Convenio 193.




ABIERTOS AL DESACUERDO




A la UNTA siempre le ha preocupado la formación y capacitación constantes por parte de las bases y de los representantes. Entendemos la necesidad de tener conversaciones complejas que pueden llegar a ser incómodas políticamente, porque estar abierto a abordar los desacuerdos hace que el sindicato sea más fuerte. 




Sin espacios de discusión y análisis se frena el desarrollo de la organización. Somos partidarios de llevar a cabo conversaciones difíciles, pero bajo ciertas reglas que permitan el diálogo y la escucha activa. Por ejemplo, para pensar temas difíciles, hay que plantear preguntas incómodas. El no estar de acuerdo con un tema no quiere decir que seamos enemigos, sino que ilustra la necesidad de pensar en los sindicatos como espacios políticos de personas que tal vez no estén de acuerdo con todo, pero que luchan juntos por metas compartidas. 




Luis Fernando Mora Reyes es secretario de Formación y Cultura del CEN de la UNTA.

author: Luis Fernando Mora Reyes
title: How We Built Our Union’s Member Education Program
content:
Earlier this year, a debate broke out among members of our union, the National App Workers Union of Mexico (UNTA), after the union’s social media post condemning the U.S. government’s kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and demanding “the defense of sovereignty, self determination and peace in Latin America.” 




Union members had conflicting views about the kidnapping, which led to a discussion on the subject in our next coordinating assembly—a space where we inform, discuss, and reach agreements between union representatives. Members disagreed intensely, but expressed their views with respect and camaraderie.


It made us realize that we needed more spaces like this for face-to-face discussion and analysis within the union, to help us develop a shared politics and grow as trade unionists. Out of these discussions, members decided to create the National Political Council (CPN), a space for debate and training on political, economic, labor, gender, and social issues.

help us think collectively about national and international issues

author: Lisa Xu
title: Reform Candidate Says UFCW Rep Tailed Him for 300 Miles to Thwart Petition Effort
content:
In a union that has been headed by one family with no competitive elections since 1984, a group of grocery workers is organizing for change. But this week, they say, union staff who back the incumbent administration went to outrageous lengths in an attempt to make sure there’s no election this year either.




On Monday afternoon, Eric Marcuz, a veteran Northern California Safeway worker, stopped at the union office to pick up blank petitions to get on the ballot in the union’s upcoming election. Marcuz is running for president on the 

At What Cost

 slate in the 23,000-member United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8-Golden State, one of the largest locals in the union.




To get on the ballot, Marcuz and his slate-mates have to collect 443 petition signatures—2 percent of the local’s active members—in the next two weeks. If they don’t get enough signatures, no election will be held.




After Marcuz picked up the petitions from the local’s Roseville office, he got in his car to drive three hours south to Fresno, to start collecting signatures with another candidate on his slate at a Save Mart store there. (The local spans a 10-hour stretch from Bakersfield up to the Oregon border). 




When Marcuz stopped for gas, he said he noticed that a black Dodge Ram pickup stopped as well. When he got back on the freeway, so did the truck.  




At the next gas stop, Marcuz spoke to the man driving the truck. It was Jeff Berns, a staff representative for Local 8-GS. His brother, Mark, is also a rep for the union—and the local’s election chair, responsible for overseeing the election. 




Marcuz asked Jeff Berns why he was following him. According to Marcuz, Berns said he wanted to make sure that all the members got the “accurate information” that Marcuz’s slate was going to “divide” the union. He said he was going to follow him the entire time Marcuz was out, all the way back to Marcuz’s house in Redding, several hours north. Marcuz jokingly asked him if he needed a place to stay. Berns said he didn’t—because he’d been staying a lot in the Redding area lately himself, which Marcuz said he thought was “creepy” because that’s where Marcuz lives with his family (and is not where Berns lives).




Berns would live up to his promise—following Marcuz for the next 300 miles, through every stop, exit, and U-turn. He even followed him inside the Fresno Save Mart, and camped out for an hour with another union rep while Marcuz ate dinner at a supporter's house 100 miles north in Modesto.




NO COMPETITIVE ELECTIONS




At the gas station, Berns repeated the mantra, “Solidarity works!” That’s the motto of the incumbent president, Jacques Loveall, who is heading the 

Solidarity Works Team

 slate in this election. 




Loveall was appointed to lead the union in 2004, when his father, Jack Loveall, stepped down. The elder Loveall had held the top office since 1984; when he retired he was one of the highest-paid union officers in the country, earning the equivalent of $1 million today. (The 

Contra Costa Times

 reported that he had a $28,000-a-year country club membership and “two pilots on staff to chauffeur him in a private jet.”) Neither father nor son has ever faced a competitive election in the local.




Back on the freeway, Marcuz called a Department of Labor agent whom he had already been in touch with. They had previously spoken about the local’s apparent attempt to 

cancel the election

 by merging with a mysterious organization called the Staffing Agencies Federated Employees, an entity which listed one of Loveall’s relatives as its president on its initial filing. The agent told him to report the intimidation to the election chair and tell him to get the rep to back off.




Marcuz then called Mark Berns, the election chair, who he said told him he would talk to staff about acting in a professional manner. 




MORE REPS




However, when Marcuz arrived at the Save Mart store in Fresno to begin collecting petition signatures, he and another slatemate, Mike Romero, said that three union reps were waiting for them, including Jeff Berns. One of the others was John Micheletti, a longtime Local 8 vice president. Far from being called off, they said, the intimidation had actually intensified.




Marcuz and Romero said the reps interfered with every conversation they attempted to have with workers about signing their nomination petition. The very first worker they engaged about signing, a longtime acquaintance of Romero’s, fled once a rep entered the conversation and became confrontational. The worker did not sign the petition.




“They were everywhere inside the store,” said Marcuz. At least one of the interactions was filmed on a phone.




Marcuz said that Berns told him, “I’m going to make sure everyone knows who you are and not to sign that.” And additionally, “We’re going to invalidate every single signature that you get.” 




It is illegal for union staff and officers to campaign on union time. Berns said he was on vacation.




Romero, who has worked at Save Mart for 30 years, said, “This is the most I’ve seen of union staff in six months.” He said a fourth rep turned up after Marcuz left.




SEEN THIS BEFORE




These tactics—following opposition candidates and invalidating signatures—have both been alleged by previous members of the local who attempted to challenge the Lovealls. 




A 

Contra Costa Times

 article published in 2004 reported that supporters of Loveall’s father got members to rescind their signatures to keep dissident candidate Jack Nordby off the ballot in 1997. A 

book

 written by then-Local 588 reform activist Doug Slaydon states that as many as 150 signatures were removed. (Local 588 merged with another local to form Local 8-GS in 2006—postponing a potential competitive election that year.) 




Nordby also alleged that he was tailed by a pickup truck while collecting ballot signatures, followed around by union reps in stores, and once, chased in his car while driving his wife and two daughters to church. 




The 

Contra Costa Times

 also reported allegations that Local 588 staffers staked out the home of a member of UFCW Local 1179 who had led a successful rank-and-file opposition campaign to an attempted merger of the two locals and “tailed him in union cars.” “In June 1994,” reported the 

Times

, the member, Michael Ross-Smith, “was rear-ended in Walnut Creek by three UFCW 588 business agents following him too closely in a white 1993 Ford Thunderbird leased to the union, according to a traffic collision report from the Walnut Creek police department.”




TAILED FOR SEVEN HOURS




Marcuz and Romero said they quickly realized that they wouldn’t be able to collect petition signatures with this level of interference. Marcuz’s next stop was going to be to drop off petition forms with a supporter at the Turlock Safeway, over an hour to the north, but he made plans to meet the supporter at their house in Modesto instead.




When Marcuz left the parking lot of the Fresno store, Romero said three vehicles followed him. Romero also realized that one of the reps had stayed behind, and he became worried that he would be followed as well. He drove around for a long time before going home, to make sure he wasn’t followed.




Marcuz, meanwhile, said that Berns and Micheletti followed him for 90 miles, all the way to Modesto. They stayed parked outside the house while Marcuz ate burritos with the supporter—finally leaving after an hour, after 8 p.m.




"It's crazy that they would literally go two hours out of their way to make sure nobody else can talk to the employees,” Romero said. 




Marcuz said he almost canceled his plans to stay alone in a hotel in Roseville overnight, worried he would be tailed there, and contemplated driving for four more hours home to Redding. In total, he estimates he was followed for seven hours, over a distance of 300 miles.




SCARE TACTICS?




Section 610 of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA) forbids the threat or use of force or violence to restrain, coerce, or intimidate union members from exercising their right to nominate candidates or to vote in union officer elections, while Section 401(e) bars “improper interference” in the rights of union members to run for and support candidates for local union office. 




“It makes me think of everyone that has known there’s been a need for change in the past, and has been scared away from pursuing it,” Marcuz said. While Marcuz and his slate are standing strong, he said, “this might work. They might intimidate and scare enough people out of participating.”




In the morning, Marcuz filed a police report with the Roseville Police Department alleging stalking and harassment, citing the time and distance he was followed and the behavior he encountered in the Fresno store. 




Local 8 did not respond to requests for comment.




Petition signatures are due November 17, and ballots will be mailed November 21.

content:

author: Dan DiMaggio
title: Book Review: A Model for U.S.-Mexico Cross-Border Solidarity
content:
Labor law reform in Mexico has opened up a major opportunity for workers fighting for genuine, independent unions. What can U.S. unions do to support our brothers and sisters there? And how can we build cross-border campaigns to confront our common employers?




Unions asking these questions will find valuable ideas in the e-book 

International Solidarity in Action: The Relationship Between the United Electrical Workers (UE) and Frente Auténtico del Trabajo (FAT)

, available for free download 

here

. 




Author Robin Alexander, retired director of international affairs for UE, led her union’s partnership with the FAT, which began in 1992, during the campaign to oppose the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).




UE members were seeing their employers cut manufacturing jobs in the U.S. and shift production to Mexico. “The UE leadership became convinced that the union needed to find a labor organization it could work with in Mexico,” Alexander writes, “and also that it was essential to connect international work more directly with UE members and with organizing.”




In a meeting in Mexico to discuss the campaign against NAFTA, the UE found the FAT—the only Mexican labor organization to oppose NAFTA.




Here was a union that had a lot in common with the left-led UE: fiercely independent, with radical roots and leadership. The FAT had long stood out against Mexico's state-dominated unions and fought for workers’ right to form genuine, independent unions.




Both unions were concerned about the growing number of jobs that corporations had moved to assembly plants near Mexico’s northern border with the United States, where unions were either nonexistent or a tool of the government’s development strategy of low wages and long hours.




“The UE,” Alexander writes, “was interested in seeing the plants organized by a union that would serve as a partner and ally in Mexico and believed that it could provide solidarity, including some leverage, where it continued to represent workers employed by those companies in the U.S… The FAT was eager to organize the plants that were moving across the border, but lacked the resources to do so.”




LIKE-MINDED UNIONS




Thus kicked off a partnership that has now lasted 30 years. The book contains several case studies of how the UE and the FAT worked together to back each other’s campaigns against employers such as General Electric and Echlin (a transnational auto parts maker later bought by Dana).




For U.S. unionists unfamiliar with the obstacles that Mexican workers are facing as they struggle to oust protection unions and replace them with genuine unions, these sections will be particularly valuable.




At Echlin, for example, workers attempting to confront dangerous exposure to asbestos and solvents and form a democratic union were met with a barrage of tactics often deployed by employers, official unions, and Mexican labor boards.




For instance, workers were refused a copy of their own collective bargaining agreement. The company fired dozens of independent union supporters, and stalled the union election by claiming the independent metal workers union did not have the proper paperwork to represent auto parts workers.




Worse, it allowed the official union to deploy 170 thugs, “some wielding metal rods, clubs, and guns,” into the plant on the eve of the election. And workers were forced to vote out loud in front of the company, official union, and labor board officials.




TWO-WAY SOLIDARITY




The UE supported the FAT’s organizing by filing complaints under NAFTA’s labor side agreement (NAALC), as well as by providing funds, pressuring shareholders, and organizing speaking tours to draw attention to workers’ rights in Mexico.




The relationship went both ways, with the FAT providing important material support to UE’s organizing efforts and fight for labor law reforms in the United States. During a UE organizing drive at a Milwaukee foundry, the FAT provided a Mexican organizer—an activist who had been fired from a GE plant in Ciudad Juarez—to help campaign among a predominantly Mexican immigrant workforce. The organizer spread the word that the UE was not like the official unions in Mexico which so many had had bad experiences with.




The FAT has also helped draw attention to the severe limitations on labor rights in states like North Carolina—home of UE Local 150, the North Carolina Public Service Workers Union—where many public sector workers are banned from collective bargaining. Mexican unions filed complaints at the International Labor Organization challenging the ban, and the ILO issued a decision that called on North Carolina to repeal it. The FAT also filed a charge under NAALC, and the Mexican government issued a favorable report in response.




While North Carolina’s ban still persists, this work has helped legitimize the union and chip away at the law’s aura of invincibility. Alexander writes, “This was tremendously energizing for the low-wage, primarily African-American workers in North Carolina’s public sector because it turned the long-held belief that public sector workers ‘just don’t have that right’ on its head: from the perspective of international human rights law, it is the state’s ban on collective bargaining that is ‘illegal,’ not workers’ attempts to assert their rights.”




WORKER TO WORKER




Part 3 of the book details worker-to-worker exchanges, which the UE and the FAT used to deepen the solidarity and “undercut the stereotypes that existed” among members on both sides of the border.




The UE-FAT exchanges happened in both the U.S. and Mexico, with an emphasis on rank-and-file participation. Members of both unions “toured plants, exchanged experiences, walked picket lines, attended meetings, assisted with organizing drives, taught high school and university classes, and participated in radio and television programs in an effort to share information, learn about each other, and take the information back to their locals and communities.”




UE Local 150 members were part of one set of exchanges where they met public sector unionists from Mexico and Quebec (the exchanges were not always just binational). The experience raised their confidence and expectations, and led to the campaign on international law.




There have also been exchanges between co-op members of both unions, organizing institutes, and cultural exchanges, including a cross-border mural project.




It showed that “the most effective way to educate workers in the United States and in Mexico—and to motivate them to educate others—was through direct contact with each other,” writes Alexander. “I still have a vivid recollection of workers bonding over their mutual outrage that instead of bonuses the company rewarded both groups by buying them pizza.”




Although social media and Zoom have made it easier to meet with people around the world, they’re no substitute for the extended, face-to-face interactions that such exchanges allow. Yet there are remarkably few such programs in place—and our labor movements are worse off because of it. Setting up more such programs should be an urgent task—and Alexander’s book provides practical advice to help.




EXPANDING OUR VISION




There’s also a glaring need for more education for U.S. unionists about what is happening in the labor movement south of the border (not to mention all over the world)—now more important than ever, as our billionaire-backed president whips up hostility against immigrants and workers abroad.




One part of UE’s solidarity work was “Mexican Labor News and Analysis,” a monthly summary that lasted from 1996 to 2016. Reviving such a project would be a real contribution to promoting an international perspective among U.S. union members. Although the UE and the FAT are both small, they have played significant roles in expanding the vision of their countries’ labor movements. 




In Mexico, where, as Alexander writes, “the FAT and their lawyers... were dismissed as dreamers who were a little crazy when they spoke of the need for secret-ballot elections, the elimination of protection contracts, independent labor judges, or registries of unions and contracts,” the 2019 labor law reform included all of those elements. 




In the U.S., the UE played a significant role in helping a then-obscure socialist candidate named Bernie Sanders win his first election to Congress in 1990, which decades later helped pave the way for Sanders to popularize an unapologetically pro-worker politics in his two presidential campaigns.




Similarly, these two unions have set out a path for international solidarity. Could more unions follow their example, and lay the foundation for a growing sense of shared struggle by U.S. and Mexican workers as a counter to the rising forces of right-wing nationalism? Alexander’s book is a great guide for anyone looking to push their unions along that path.			     




A longer version of this article first appeared in 

New Labor Forum

.

author: Sarah Hughes
title: Members Alarmed by End-Run around Democracy at Buffalo Health Care Local
content:
Things had been tense for some time inside the leadership of Communications Workers (CWA) Local 1168, a 4,800-member health care union based near Buffalo, New York. Still, it was a high-functioning local with a busy calendar of events, stewards handling grievances, organizers pursuing leads, and leaders organizing at work.




So it was a surprise to members in June when their parent union, CWA, put the local into trusteeship, at the request of the local’s president and seven of the nineteen executive board members.




Trusteeship meant the union’s bylaws and elected leaders were suspended, and most of its work temporarily ground to a halt. The appointed Director of Organizing and Mobilizing Mary Nowocien and elected Vice President Patrick Weisansal II found themselves locked out of their group chats, email, and union hall, and facing an internal union prosecution.




A staffer of CWA District 1, Erin Spaulding, was assigned as trustee—tasked with maintaining the functioning of the local, setting up and overseeing judicial processes for the charges against officers, and making a plan to return the union to local control.




Nowocien and Weisansal saw the sudden trusteeship as an escalation of a long-running conflict and a deliberate undermining of the upcoming union elections. Weisansal had just announced his intention to run against incumbent President Cori Gambini. 




Now the elections are on hold until the trials are over, whenever that is. And lately, the employer has been taking advantage of the turmoil in the union. 




While the allegations are serious, members are concerned that the trusteeship was a nuclear option for an internal financial matter and that it has torn apart relationships at the local, weakened opposition to management’s schemes and denied democratic processes to an active, engaged union membership.  




ALLEGED TIMECARD ISSUES




The trusteeship filing lists the cause as “serious allegations of financial misconduct” from officers and “dueling charges” between leaders. 




Gambini and Executive Vice President Robert Andruszko had accused Nowocien and Weisansal of defrauding the local of thousands of dollars, by getting paid by both the union and their employer for the same hours worked, and by falsifying records. These issues came to light during a timecard audit in the fall of 2025 by their employer, Kaleida Health. 




Nowocien and Weisansal acknowledged there were significant errors on old timecards and paychecks, but said it was the product of the employer’s faulty timekeeping and payroll system, and human error. The majority of other officers also had issues, they pointed out, but only some were being singled out for discipline by the local and the employer. 




Spaulding, the trustee, interviewed all the suspended officers and allowed the majority to return to their paid positions—with the exception of Nowocien, Weisansal, and three others not facing any charges: the Communications and Political Directors and one of the Area Vice Presidents. Also fired were two longtime staff organizers, on the grounds that there was no work for them to do, according to one, Ann Converso, who had recently helped organize a new unit of substance use disorder counselors and was gearing up for their first contract fight. 




Many current leaders on both sides of this schism were part of a reform caucus in Local 1168, the Caucus of Rank-and-File Healthcare Employees (CORHE), which dissolved when they won their positions in 2020.




Since winning, Gambini and a few others have butted heads with Weisansal, Nowocien, and others over how to tackle problems. The latter camp frequently organized their facility—Buffalo General Hospital, the union’s largest unit—to push back against management’s changes and violations. Gambini and leaders aligned with her argued that that wasn’t the right approach—that they had to pick their fights and not overextend the membership, according to Weisansal.




One Buffalo General steward, who asked to not be named, said members were appalled that the trustee had removed elected officers. “If our employer treated one of our members in a similar fashion,” the steward said, “union leadership would rally around them and fight to return them to their position!”




Spaulding wrote in a public FAQ posted on the local’s social media that the temporary administration “is not intended to be punitive or find guilt against any individual in the Local. It is intended to stabilize the Local while issues are investigated and resolved.” She also wrote that staffing decisions were made based on “operational needs of the local, nature of pending charges, and interviews conducted with each board member [by the trustee].”




CWA, Spaulding, and Gambini did not respond to requests for comment. Re-instated Area Vice President Kim Kornowski emailed 

Labor Notes

, writing, “we are a democratic union that includes our members in all aspects of our work. In 2020, we ran together on the C.O.R.H.E. slate and implemented our platform. A few board members engaged in serious financial misconduct, and we requested that the local be placed under trusteeship while these issues are addressed.” 




A THOUSAND SIGNATURES




Some of the former members of CORHE re-formed as a committee and started reaching out to members. They drafted a petition to the trustee, asking for a general membership meeting, an end to the trusteeship, a neutral election to be held this fall, and for the elected officers to be returned to their positions in the meantime. In the local’s bylaws, if 20 percent of the members (around 1000 people) request a meeting, leadership is compelled to hold one. 




The members of the reorganized CORHE worked to get the petition signed: they printed paper copies, talked to co-workers, and asked colleagues in different units to gather signatures.




Weisansal said he appealed to people’s commitment to union democracy. “The in-person membership meeting we were supposed to have got canceled,” he said. “There’s been a lot of anger about the [virtual] town hall calls, [because] they filter the questions. People aren’t stupid, and they're angry.




“What has been helpful is not asking people to be the judge or jury,” he said. “What we’re asking is, do you believe in democracy, and if members should be able to make decisions about their own union.”




Nowocien and Weisensal are well-known union activists, so many members were eager to sign on in their defense. “There are still a lot of good people in this union that see how wrong this is all going,” said Ashley Emminger, a mobilizer at Buffalo General. “They just want this [trusteeship] to end, to have the people we elected back where they belong, and elections move forward.” 




Weisansal and Nowocien have had to fight for their positions before. In 2019 they were removed from the Local 1168 board by a previous leadership, they say in retaliation for their organizing. (Gambini was not present for that vote, and fought for them to be reinstated.) At that time, they gathered the signatures to compel a membership meeting, 200 people showed up to support them, and the two were returned to their positions. The following year, Weisansal won the vice presidency and Nowocien was appointed to her special director role.




By camping out in cafeterias and parking garages, the committee collected 1,000 signatures within a few weeks. Kaleida management called a few petition-gatherers into investigatory meetings for using company space and “harassing” members. The petitioners maintained that their activities were legally protected, but they moved the petition-gathering online after that. (Kaleida declined to comment on these meetings.)




Weisansal emailed the 1,000 signatures to the trustee, to CWA District 1, and to the national CWA leadership in September. However, with the bylaws suspended, the trustee was not compelled to hold a membership meeting, and the caucus received a notice from District 1 deferring to the trustee. 




The Buffalo General steward said co-workers who signed feel as if their voices don’t matter. 




LEADERS FIRED




Shortly after the petition was sent in, Nowocien and Weisansal got word that they were being investigated again by the employer, Kaleida Health, for similar instances of timecard irregularities, but going back to 2024, spurred by the union’s investigations. 




Then they were both terminated for 2024 timecard issues.




Weisansal thinks the case is weak: he has 16 years of service and no disciplinary record, and was fired just now for a paperwork error he had already communicated to his manager about. Nowocien has 20 years of service at Buffalo General.




Now, while Weisansal and Nowocien focus on their wrongful termination cases, other caucus members are continuing to speak up about workplace issues, bring in new members, and push for elections to be scheduled.




A third CORHE leader was fired right before publication of this article, apparently for one timecard infraction. 




Kaleida had already audited timecards for 19 union board members and appointed directors in 2025, and found discrepancies for 16 of them. 

Labor Notes

 obtained a copy of the spreadsheet that Kaleida Human Resources sent to the board delineating the errors and the action to be taken by members and employer to remedy the errors. Several of those officers paid back amounts they had over-received, or were compensated by Kaleida Health for 2025 errors, according to Nowocien and Weisansal.




No one received disciplinary action at the time, and the comments in the spreadsheet show that management was aware that its timekeeper system was to blame for the majority of the errors. Only Nowocien and Weisansal were investigated for timecard issues prior to 2025.




Kaleida declined to comment on its timekeeping system or the process of reconciling errors.




It was after Kaleida’s first investigation that Gambini moved, in fall of 2025, to open up a union investigation into timecard issues as well. The board agreed to spend $10,000 on an auditor, but the findings were never released to the board, according to Nowocien and others. However, the president singled out Weisansal and Nowocien, and warned them that union disciplinary action could be coming for their discrepancies.




Then in May 2026, just before the trusteeship, Weisensal and Nowocien said that President Gambini encouraged them to resign from the board and forfeit their memberships, threatening that otherwise the FBI and Department of Labor would get involved and that they would be banned from holding any CWA position in the future. They declined, they said, because they had not seen any written charges or specifics about the accusations.




Local 1168 has hired two more auditors since October 2025, and members are awaiting the results. Emminger, the mobilizer at Buffalo General, is upset with the lack of transparency and the spending of member’s dues: “They have not been transparent about anything.” 




REVERBERATIONS AT WORK




A smart employer knows: Never waste a crisis. Patients and staff at Kaleida Health may notice the effects of a distracted CWA 1168.




“Kaleida is 100 percent capitalizing on this dysfunction to push through changes,” Weisansal said.




Converso, the organizer laid off after 16 years, said “if we [Nowocien and Converso] were still there, we would be in the streets with everything Kaleida is doing.”




One change includes getting rid of a cardiac monitoring unit and shifting around the responsibility for heart monitoring to circumvent the 1:4 nurse-to-patient ratio mandated by the staffing committee and contract.




Emminger voted for the CORHE slate in 2020 and then got heavily involved in the union because of their organizing focus. She says there has been no mobilization since the trusteeship, when before they would have been pushing back against the short staffing.




“This tells the employer that staffing is not a priority, and this will harm us in the next contract,” she said “They are taking full advantage of this witch hunt, and the proof is in the department changes and job deletions.” 




The changes will mean more work for nursing staff and less oversight of patients with serious heart problems, according to Nowocien and former Area Vice President Jennifer Hogue, another of the five removed officers. Kaleida declined to comment. 




Hogue has been telling members they can fight back against these changes, even without the support of union leadership: “We are not giving the employer a free pass to do whatever they want.”




…AND BEYOND




But the reverberations also extend beyond Local 1168’s own shops. The union has been an important force in the local labor movement, and especially a support to its sister union, CWA Local 1133.




Labor Notes

 profiled

 Local 1133’s strike in 2021 at Mercy Health, where it represents 2,000 health care workers; Local 1168 represents smaller units in the same chain, Catholic Health. Though the contract barred them from striking all at once, leaders and staff like Weisansal and Converso were “loaned” to Local 1133 to help build the organizing capacity of the strike, which won safer staffing ratios.




“I wouldn’t have survived our strike without any of those three [Nowocien, Weisansal, and Converso],” said now-retired Local 1133 mobilizer Bob Scime. “They were rocks for me personally, and our whole local, and they kept our lines going. I always feel a sense of gratitude to them.




“I can say the same thing about Erin [Spaulding, the trustee] when we were on strike, she was a rock too, and Cori [Gambini, the president], too. Sign of the labor movement today, that we’re fighting among ourselves. It’s the members who are suffering for it,” said Scime.




The bargaining teams and leaders of 1133 and 1168 have organized for the last few years to line up their contract expiration dates, so any future strikes could be coordinated and leverage power for health care workers in Buffalo. Their next contract expiration is in May 2028, when Weisansal had hoped that Local 1168 would join in United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain’s call for coordinated labor action. 




As the seasons change, Hogue, the former Membership Functions Chair, is also grieving the loss of an annual tradition: the CWA 1168 Halloween Party. “Normally this is a community where people feel like they belong,” she said.

author: Unknown
title: Bottom-Up Organizing: How We Got Clean Porta-Johns
content:
The first day I showed up on the Marriott construction site in downtown Detroit, everyone warned me about the state of our bathrooms. 




You could smell them halfway across most floors. They were full in 24 hours, urinals were often clogged, and some people had taken to using buckets and hiding them in closets. 




Every electrician already had the same idea: we wanted the cleaning schedule changed from twice a week to three times.




I had a long conversation with the steward about what had been tried. The first instinct of a construction worker is to “drag” (quit), drive over to the union hall, and pick up a new job. As expected, there was a steady trickle of drags, but no improvement to conditions.




OSHA had been called and walked the site, only to say that the number of bathrooms was up to their standard. The electrical contractor had been notified, but because the bathrooms were for all the trades, our bosses didn’t feel it was their responsibility to pay for additional cleaning. 




Our Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 58 contract only gestures vaguely to “sanitary facilities,” and protects us explicitly should we leave the site to find a “sanitary” facility. This clause was exercised regularly, but no one could say for sure whether the boss was even aware we were leaving.

author: Kari Thompson
title: The First-Ever California State Workers’ Strike
content:
State workers went on a one-day unfair labor practice strike across California October 21, with picket lines in Sacramento, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and other cities. They're demanding better pay, affordable health care coverage, and flexibility to work from home. 




This was the first strike in the history of SEIU Local 1000, which represents about 100,000 government employees, ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses at state offices, hospitals, and prisons. 




They have been working without a contract since July 1. Some 5,000 employees were 

excluded

 from striking.




Governor Gavin Newsom’s “return-to-office” mandate went into effect this past summer. It requires workers to be in the office four days per week—even though workers report there isn’t enough space for all of them.




Workers argue the return-to-work policy compounds the lack of pay increases. Being forced back into the office is “more than just a pay cut,” said Jonah Paul, who works for the Employment Development Department in Sacramento. ”It’s a huge reduction in quality of life.




“Telework is a stopgap for a lot of problems our society is not willing to address,” Paul said: “the cost of childcare, and insane commutes. Telework becomes a catch-all solution for a grueling life.”




ZERO RAISE




Last year, Local 1000 agreed to a pay freeze to help the state meet a budget shortfall. This summer, however, workers were supposed to see raises. But they got zilch.




The union is asking for a 20 percent raise over three years to catch up, especially given increased state revenue over the past two years.




Though Local 1000 and the state have met several times to negotiate a new contract, the union says CalHR, the bargaining representative for the state, has not been negotiating in good faith. It filed unfair labor practice charges with the state Public Employment Relations Board against CalHR for delaying negotiations and failing to respond to proposals.




“When I first started working for the state 10 years ago, for the most part CalHR would throw us a bone,” said steward Giovanni Martinez, a state worker in Sacramento. “This is the worst bargaining cycle I’ve witnessed. They don’t want to budge on a lot of stuff. Newsom takes us for granted, and the people he’s appointed in CalHR are the same way.”




Under previous leadership, the union 

kicked in $1 million

 to help Newsom fight a recall campaign in 2021. Members question why a governor they supported doesn’t have their backs now.




STRIKE SCHOOLS




Members of Local 1000 have been organizing over the past few months to increase membership numbers. Activists have been approaching nonmembers at their own worksites to ask them personally to join the union, and calling others on the phone.




Stewards did their best to increase communications across the membership, though they were hampered by limited updates from the official Bargaining Unit Negotiating Committee.




Paul said that three years ago, the local offered “strike schools” to members, but these were more about discouraging members from planning for a strike. This time, he said, strike schools emphasized that the decision to strike was one for members to make, building membership numbers along with enthusiasm for walking out together.




In a strike authorization vote held from September 9 to October 7, 96 percent voted “yes” to walk out.




On the final day of the vote, the union held informational pickets to encourage participation in the vote. One picket happened to be next door to a building where Newsom was giving a speech.




With just a half-hour’s notice, stewards and other union leaders managed to get members together to cover every entrance of the building and make enough noise that Newsom had to comment on it during his event.




Despite this pressure from members, there was no last-minute deal to avert the strike, as happened 10 years ago under Governor Jerry Brown.




“For a lot of folks this is their first strike—this is mine,” Martinez said. ”We didn’t want to walk off the job—we have a good relationship with our supervisors—but we had no choice.”




WORLD’S FOURTH-LARGEST ECONOMY




Strike participation appeared strong, with thousands of workers joining rallies and marches in cities across the state. Striking workers in the state’s capitol shut down multiple blocks with a march from CalHR headquarters to the capitol building.




“I was up on the truck with our president and a few other folks, leading people to different rally points,” said Emily Ingram, a Department of Education worker in Sacramento. “All you could see in every direction was more people. It was a pretty powerful feeling.”




In Los Angeles, hundreds of workers rallied outside a state building. Arielle Mangabat-Lowe, who works at the Department of Toxic Substances Control, said she was surprised how many people showed up, after prior actions had only a few dozen participants. She reflected that it can be hard as an organizer to put so much work into the union without knowing whether other members will participate. 




But being with others at the strike rally boosted her spirits. “The state of California is a terrifying employer—it’s the world’s fourth-largest economy. We showed up today anyways,” she said. “It’s cool to feel like you have a voice, especially in these times.”




“As someone who has been trying to get folks to join up, I think a lot of state workers are fired up,” said Martinez. “The energy is here. Where we go with it, that’s up to us as members and our leadership.” 




The union continued to pressure CalHR after the strike. On October 27, about 20 members disrupted a CalHR event in Sacramento, distributing flyers and shouting a message to the crowd demanding that the state stop intimidating members and bargain fairly.




The two sides are scheduled for contract mediation on October 30, but members are skeptical that the state will come ready to negotiate a deal. “We are continuing to prepare for another strike if needed,” Ingram said.

author: Lisa Xu
title: UFCW Members Protect Local Election After Sham Merger Attempt
content:
An insurgent slate is challenging the longtime incumbents in Local 8-Golden State, one of the largest locals in the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), in what may be the local’s first competitive election in decades. And now, after protecting the election from a sham merger attempt that would have canceled the election, the battle is on. 




Ballots are set to be mailed on November 21. But when members first saw the election notice in the local’s newsletter, they discovered a big “but.” The notice stated that the election would not proceed if Local 8 merged with another union, the 

Staffing Agencies Federated Employees

 (SAFE), before the end of the year. 




Members said they had never heard about this possible merger, or SAFE, before reading about it in the final sentence of the election notice, mailed to members on October 16. 




What is SAFE? Publicly available information about the organization, which has multiple ties to Local 8 President Jacques Loveall, raised more questions than answers. Neither Local 8, the UFCW International union, nor SAFE has responded to inquiries about the merger.

author: Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Mexico Volkswagen Workers Could Soon Strike
content:
In Mexico, at the world’s largest Volkswagen facility outside of Germany, workers are weighing the risks of a possible strike.




The 6,500 workers build the Jetta, Tiguan, and Taos at the company’s Puebla plant. Their union, SITIAVW, is one of Mexico’s most storied independent unions, and is in the midst of the plant’s annual wage reopener negotiations.




Days before the strike deadline of October 22, the company presented two proposals—offering raises of 7.98 percent and 7.95 percent for a one-year duration—which were rejected by the union. Soon afterwards, the company presented another offer: an 8.24 percent increase, of which 3.59 percent is a one-time payment of 12,000 pesos, equivalent to about $641 U.S. The deal would maintain the yearly salary reopener, a cycle the company had tried to lengthen in previous offers. Workers will vote on the offer on October 28, and could strike the next day if a deal is not reached. 




On October 15, workers voted down an offer that  would have provided a 13 percent combined increase to wages and benefits over the next two years. The vote was 3,135 against and 2,452 for.

author: Jenny Brown
title: Tampa TSA Union Averted   Privatization Disaster
content:
TSA agents noticed something was up. “We started seeing people around the airport that you wouldn’t normally see, people in suits,” said Mark Harris, Transportation Security Officer and union steward in Tampa, Florida.  




That’s when he realized the airport was a target for the TSA privatization program he had been reading about—the $13 billion Gold+ program. Harris, and his union Government Employees (AFGE) Local 556, swung into action. 




Transportation Security Administration workers have been winning battles lately. Twice in two years the Trump administration has tried to cancel their union contract, and twice it has been stopped by the courts. Now things are mostly back to normal, with the contract in force and grievances being processed.




But Gold+ would undermine the union by outsourcing TSO jobs to private companies. As the dimensions of the plan became clear, Harris said his co-workers “felt like they had been kicked in the gut. You know, everything that they had worked for, their federal pension, careers, everything.”




Tampa is a model airport that consistently ranks at the top in customer satisfaction. That’s why TSA picked it for the Gold+ privatization effort, Harris said. “They don’t want to give it to a poor airport or a failing airport. That would be disastrous for TSA, right?”

author: Caitlyn Clark
title: Interview: How We Beat Back Nonunion Subcontracting at Kroger
content:
After more than six months fighting against Kroger’s use of non-union subcontractors, members of Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 700 in Indiana won a 

victory

 in August, when Kroger announced it would be ending the Retail Odyssey direct store delivery (DSD) program entirely.




This means more hours for union members—thanks to those who organized to enforce the contract, file grievances, and educate their co-workers. In this interview conducted by Caitlyn Clark of the reform group Essential Workers for Democracy, shop stewards Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson explain how they did it.




Essential Workers for Democracy: What is Retail Odyssey and why is it a problem? 




Andrea Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey is a nonunion third-party contractor that solely services Kroger stores. Normally RO does things like rearranging a store layout or auditing whether products are displayed the way the brand wants.




A few months ago, the Kroger Central Division here in Indiana developed a new program utilizing RO employees to stock direct store delivery vendor items on weekends. [

DSD items are delivered straight to the store by the supplier, rather than coming through a Kroger warehouse.

]




Why is this a problem? Kroger has employees who need hours. This isn't “extra help.” Kroger wants to phase nonunion third parties into the stores to cut hours of its union employees.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Labor Goes on Election Defense
content:
New York City unions representing 1 million members launched a new coalition October 15 to defend the right to vote ahead of the midterm elections November 3. A thousand members rallied outside the city’s main post office, pledging to mobilize the labor movement to defend the elections from Trump administration interference. 




The throng included large contingents from Laborers Locals 78 and 79, the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, building services and airport workers from SEIU 32BJ, and health care workers from 1199SEIU. There were also union telecom workers, nurses, stagehands, municipal workers, retail workers, postal workers, electricians, grocery workers, office workers, and painters. 




The NYC Central Labor Council initiative, called “Our Voice, Our Vote, Our Democracy,” aims to turn out union members and their communities to protest peacefully and to document intimidation of voters. It was announced just ahead of October 17, when the No Kings coalition held 3,000 events nationwide to promote early voting.




“We are demanding democratic and fair elections,” said SEIU 32BJ President Manny Pastreich in a statement to 

Labor Notes

. “In anticipation of possible election sabotage, unions have hosted dozens of know-your-rights trainings, have organized hundreds of poll-watchers, and have created rapid-response networks.”

author: Unknown
title: Book Review: Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line
content:
Union strength or weakness is often seen only through the light of a strike or lockout. Phil Cohen’s memoir, 

Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line

, tells a different story. Union building is on-going, from organizing to win a first contract, to maintaining and strengthening that contract over time, from grievance handling to arbitration, from safety and health to pension rights. And in every situation there is a need to build membership participation, develop and support local leadership, strengthen mutual support, ensure understanding of rights, understanding of power and how to wield it (or lose it). 




Cohen demonstrates as much as he explains how every aspect of the above is at the heart of a union’s ability to improve conditions on the job, improve pay and benefits, and ultimately be able to win on the picket line if it comes to that.




A chapter recalling fighting back against a union-busting attorney during bargaining is emblematic. BTR Sealing Systems in Reidsville, North Carolina—a factory making wiper blades for auto companies—negotiated a first contract with workers after the plant was organized in 1995. Frequent grievances and conflicts with supervisors were part of the reality where both workers and frontline supervisors were unfamiliar with negotiating day-to-day disputes via a contract. title: Trabajadores de la salud de Iowa exigen el regreso de una compañera deportada
content:
Fatou Traore se dirigía a su trabajo como personal de limpieza en los Hospitales y Clínicas de la Universidad de Iowa (UIHC) en la mañana del jueves 24 de septiembre, cuando agentes de ICE la detuvieron. 




A pesar de tener estatus migratorio legal en Estados Unidos, y sin antecedentes penales, fue deportada a Sierra Leone—un lugar con el que no tiene ningún vínculo—el 12 de octubre. Traore es una querida integrante de la comunidad de Iowa City, y del Local 12 del Consejo 61 de AFSCME. También es madre de cuatro hijos, el menor de los cuales tiene solo tres años. 




Cuando aprendí que fue detenida en Septiembre, me indignó que ICE se había llevado a alguien del mero hospital donde yo trabajaba. Muchos de los trabajadores en el hospital no sabían de su detención, o temían alzar la voz. author: Unknown
title: Iowa Hospital Workers Demand Return of Deported Co-Worker
content:
Fatou Traore was on her way to work as a custodian at the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics (UIHC) on the morning of Thursday, September 24, when ICE agents detained her. 




Despite having legal immigration status in the United States and no criminal record, she was deported to Sierra Leone (a place she has no connection to) on October 12. Traore is a beloved member of the Iowa City community and of AFSCME Council 61, Local 12. She is also the mother of four children, the youngest of whom is three years old.




When I first heard the news of her September detention, I was upset that ICE had taken someone from the very hospital where I worked. Many of the workers at the hospital weren’t aware of her detention or were afraid to speak up. I wrote to all of the inpatient phlebotomists I used to work with at main campus, some of whom had also been custodians and worked with Fatou. 




I wrote an opinion letter for a local paper, 

Little Village

. I helped spread the word to raise awareness of her detention across community networks, from my supervisors and senior administration at UIHC, to the soccer team that my son plays on, to the yoga community I belong to, to my own family and their church communities, to the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, which I graduated from in 2022—to every person that I knew.
